summary: Discusses what it means to be on the Internet and gives terminology to distinguish levels of access for service consumers and providers. It is informational.

eli5.summary: Names for the different ways of being connected, from just visiting to running a service.

questions: what does on the internet mean
what does it mean to be on the internet
subtitle: Four ways users connect to and participate in the Internet.

tldr.problem: As the Internet grew, it became unclear what it meant for a user or organization to be "on" the Internet, because different levels of access provided very different capabilities.
tldr.mechanism: Crocker defines four categories of access, from most to least: Full Access (permanent TCP/IP connection with servers), Client Access (running applications locally but with limited connectivity), Mediated Access (running applications on a service provider's system), and Messaging Access (email and news only).
tldr.outcome: These terms provide clarity for Internet consumers and providers when discussing what connectivity capabilities are needed, and help distinguish between different business models and user scenarios.

today: RFC 1775 is Informational and has not been obsoleted. These four categories remain useful conceptual distinctions, although the prevalence of broadband, mobile networks, and VPNs has shifted the distribution of users across these categories since 1995.

sections.title: Levels of Internet Access
sections.content:
David Crocker observes that the Internet has grown to support many different types of users and access scenarios. The question "Is this user on the Internet?" became ambiguous, because connectivity can take many forms with very different implications for what the user can do.

The RFC defines four access categories, ordered from most to least capability. These distinctions are practical and user-focused: they describe what applications a user can run and the visibility and reliability of their connection.
sections.eli5: When people started connecting to the Internet in different ways, they got confused about whether someone was really "on" it or not. This RFC sorts out four clear ways.

sections.title: The Four Access Categories
sections.content:
Full Access: A permanent, full-time connection running TCP/IP, operated by Internet service providers. Machines with Full access are directly visible to the rest of the Internet via ping and other discovery tools. The core of the Internet comprises systems with Full access.

Client Access: Users run Internet applications on their own computer, such as a web browser or email client, but may have limited or intermittent connectivity (for example, via dial-up or through a firewall). Client users may not always be visible to the Internet.

Mediated Access: The user runs no Internet applications directly. Instead, a service provider runs the applications on a server and the user accesses them through a simplified interface, such as a terminal dial-up. The user is "on" the Internet, but their computer is not.

Messaging Access: The user has only email and news access. Messaging services can carry other protocols at high latency, making them useful for certain types of interaction, though not for real-time services.
sections.eli5: Full: your own 24/7 phone line. Client: you run apps but maybe not always on. Mediated: you call a helper who calls the Internet. Messaging: you only get mail and newspapers.

sections.title: Real-World Scenarios
sections.content:
A home user who dials into a service provider to use a terminal is using Mediated access; the service provider has Client or Full access, but the user does not. By contrast, users connecting via SLIP or PPP protocols run Internet applications on their own computers and have Client access.

A corporation with a full-time Internet link has Full access. Users within that corporation using web browsers through a firewall have Client access. However, if the corporation requires all Internet access to go through a special administration machine, users connecting to that machine have Mediated access.
sections.eli5: A home dial-up user is mediated: the helper (ISP) is on the Internet, the user is not. A corporate office with a full link has Full access. Someone in that office using a browser has Client access. Someone forced to use a special admin machine has Mediated access.
